findings.label: per-call host launch gap dominates every workload up to 1M elements

evidence.metric: kernel median duration vs inter-launch interval median
kernel duration vs inter-launch interval (1M fp16)

findings.inference: Device execution is only about 2 percent of the 75us walltime for 1024 elements, and the kernel for 1M elements (34-40us) still fits inside the same 75us floor. The flat floor across 1K and 1M elements proves a per-call host cost, not element work.

findings.label: 4096x4096 case is scalar/issue bound, not MTE bandwidth bound

evidence.metric: kernel duration fp16 vs fp32 at 2x bytes

findings.inference: DMA engines are idle about 85 percent of the kernel and doubling moved bytes adds only 2us, so the 16384-program kernel is not MTE bandwidth bound. The instruction listing shows roughly 190 mapped instructions per 1024-element program with only about 30 vector operations and repeated per-block barrier and flag stalls, so issue/scalar work dominates.

data.performance_interpretation: Nine of the twelve timing workloads sit at a 75-87us host-side floor while their kernels run only 1.3-40us, so their measured speedups (0.13-0.16) are set by per-call dispatch overhead against an 11.2-12.8us torch reference. The three 4096x4096 cases are device-bound near 600us with scalar ratio 0.59-0.66, vector ratio 0.13-0.18 and MTE ratios 0.12-0.16, i.e. an instruction-issue limit in a 16384-program grid of 1024-element blocks rather than a memory limit. Effective bandwidth computed from eval latency and algorithmic bytes is about 112 GB/s for fp16 and 223 GB/s for fp32, far below any plausible HBM ceiling and not a Roofline claim.

findings.label: Per-call launch cost dominates all nine workloads with numel <= 1M; the device kernel occupies only 5-19% of the period

evidence.metric: avg kernel duration _log10_nomask (1024 fp16, 100 invocations, min 1.08 / max 3.70)
mean kernel start-to-start interval (tasks 2..111, 109 intervals, span 2433.27us)
mean kernel start-to-start interval (tasks 2..111, 109 intervals, span 2668.63us)

findings.inference: For fp16/1024 the profiled device stream shows a mean 22.3us start-to-start period around a 1.2-1.5us kernel, i.e. about 94% of the period the stream is idle waiting for the next submission; eval latency for the same workload is 19.44us (reference 10.50us). At 1M elements the kernel grows to 4.6us but the period grows to 24.5us, so the host still sets the pace. The profiled periods exceed eval latency by 2-5us, which is consistent with msprof instrumentation overhead, so these intervals are an upper bound on the host cost, not a direct measurement of it. Because eval latency (~18-20us) minus kernel time (1.5-4.6us) leaves ~15-18us unaccounted, at least 75% of the eval latency on these nine workloads is outside kernel execution. The device artifacts cannot separate a Python-level wrapper from the pybind/CANN launch from the harness dispatch; that split is unresolved and is the object of the next experiment.

findings.label: The three 4096x4096 workloads are AIV-bound at ~96% with strictly additive (non-overlapped) pipelines

evidence.metric: mean kernel start-to-start interval equals kernel duration for fp16 4096x4096 (tasks 3..11: 290.045us / 8)

findings.inference: In all three large cases the AIV pipeline times sum to ~100% of aiv_time (fp16 35.07/34.83, bf16 37.15/36.91, fp32 37.86/37.64), and aiv_time is 96% of kernel duration, while per-invocation values are constant to within 1.5% across 100 calls. Additive pipeline occupancy of ~100% means the block load (MTE2), vector compute, and store (MTE3) of the single 32768-element tile are effectively serialized rather than overlapped; the kernel is a single load/compute/store with 512 programs and no cross-tile pipelining. Their start-to-start interval equals kernel duration (36.26us vs 36.23us), so these three workloads are already device-bound and no further host reduction can help them.

findings.label: fp16/bf16 4096x4096 pay ~7-9us of extra vector time for the fp32 detour at identical element and program count

evidence.metric: vec_time 20.169us (ratio 0.579) for fp16, 16777216 elems, 512 programs, BLOCK 32768
vec_time 12.959us (ratio 0.344) for fp32, same 16777216 elems and same 512 programs
mte2/mte3 are byte-proportional (fp16 5.660/6.267 vs fp32 10.157/11.990), confirming identical tile/program structure

findings.inference: Element count, program count (Block Num 512) and tile are identical across the fp16 and fp32 runs, and the transfer times scale exactly with bytes, so the +7.2us of vector time in fp16 (and +9.3us in bf16) is attributable to the two dtype conversions around the fp32 log (x.to(float32) and the narrowing store) rather than to more log evaluations or a different tiling. The reference behaves the same way in the opposite direction: its fp16 4096x4096 latency is 15.89us while its bf16 latency is 25.37us, which suggests the reference performs log natively in fp16 but must upcast for bf16. Instruction-level confirmation was not obtained: the instruction collection for this kernel failed with the simulator deadline expiring, so the conversion attribution rests on the pipeline-counter comparison only.

findings.label: A vendor aclnn elementwise kernel overlaps MTE2/MTE3 on the same 4096x4096 fp16 shape, proving overlap is reachable on this device

evidence.metric: aclnnAdds_AddAiCore_Add on 4096x4096 fp16: duration 20.941us, aiv 17.883, mte2 10.953 (0.612), mte3 11.903 (0.666), vec 2.423 (0.135) -> ratios sum 1.50
aclnnAbs_AbsAiCore_Abs on 4096x4096 fp16: duration 32.080us, aiv 28.493, mte2 21.792 (0.765), mte3 15.665 (0.550)

findings.inference: On the same device and the same 4096x4096 fp16 shape, the vendor Adds kernel shows pipeline ratios summing to 1.50 (mte2 10.95 + mte3 11.90 exceed aiv_time 17.88), i.e. its transfers genuinely overlap each other and its compute, whereas the candidate's ratios sum to ~1.00. The Adds kernel moves more bytes than the in-place log10 (two reads plus a write versus one read plus one write) yet completes in 20.9us against the candidate's 36.2us, so a ~1.7x overlap gain on the same shape is demonstrated on this hardware. This comparison is indicative, not a matched control: Adds is a pure copy-like op with 2.4us of vector work and it ran in the harness correctness path rather than the timed loop, so it cannot be used to predict the exact log10 gain.

data.performance_interpretation: The round-2 change worked: geo_mean rose 0.110 -> 0.602 and the 4096x4096 latencies fell 0.60ms -> 0.036-0.039ms, and the profile confirms the device side now matches the eval timing exactly on those three shapes (kernel 36.2/38.3/39.1us versus eval 36.0/38.1/39.0us). Two distinct regimes remain. (1) All nine workloads with numel <= 1M are launch-bound: the device kernel is only 1.5-4.6us while eval latency is 17.8-20.2us, and the profiled stream shows a 22-24.5us start-to-start period around that kernel. The reference reaches 10.5-12.1us end-to-end through the same harness, which proves a materially cheaper per-call path is achievable and bounds what is left on the table at roughly 0.75-1.0x for those nine. (2) The three 4096x4096 workloads are device-bound with serialized pipelines; the fp16 case is the weakest (0.441) because its vector time is 20.2us versus 13.0us for fp32 at the same element count, and because nothing overlaps (~7us of that is spent below fp32). Effective byte rates implied by the authoritative eval latencies are about 1.85 TB/s (fp16 large, 67MB/36.0us), 1.76 TB/s (bf16 large) and 3.44 TB/s (fp32 large), against 4.0-4.2 TB/s implied by the reference on the same shapes; these are arithmetic ratios from eval latency and total bytes, not measured bandwidth and not a roofline claim. Neither the 168MB L2 size nor these rates establish a hardware ceiling. The dominant bound for the round as a whole is launch, because it governs nine of twelve workloads and at least 75% of their latency.

next_experiment.action_description: Attack the residual per-call host cost on the cached fast path, in two steps. (a) Bounded debug probe first, to avoid spending an eval round blind: time a loop of the current cached closure, a bare pybind call with all arguments pre-bound and the stream value already resolved, a variant that passes the data pointer as an int instead of the tensor object, and an empty Python loop, all on a 1024-element fp16 tensor without per-iteration synchronisation. That isolates Python-wrapper cost, argument marshalling, and the CANN launch itself. (b) Then shrink the per-call path in main.py to a single dict lookup plus one pybind call: fold dtype, numel and the alignment bit into a two-level cache so no data_ptr()/contiguous()/dtype attribute work happens on a hit, remove the intermediate launch() Python frame by calling the bound launcher inline in run() with grid/function/metadata already bound, and keep the ordinary Triton launch as the cold/misaligned/non-contiguous fallback. Do not cache the numeric stream across calls without validating it against torch.npu.current_stream(); the no-wait raw-stream getter must stay per call or be identity-checked.
next_experiment.expected_impact: The nine sub-1M workloads sit at 17.8-20.2us against a 10.5-12.1us reference, with only 1.5-4.6us of that being kernel. Removing 3-5us of per-call host cost should move them to roughly 14-16us, i.e. speedups from 0.54-0.67 toward 0.70-0.85, which is a geo_mean of about 0.72-0.78 versus 0.602; if the probe shows the cost is dominated by argument marshalling and the int-pointer variant is materially faster, the upper end of that range is reachable. The three 4096x4096 workloads are device-bound and must come out unchanged.
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: Main risks: (1) dropping the per-call alignment check could send misaligned tensors down the unmasked 32768-tile path and break correctness for slices, so alignment must be decided at cache-build time with the masked/standard launch retained as fallback; (2) replacing the per-call stream getter with a cached value would break under a stream switch, so keep the current accessor or validate stream identity; (3) in-place semantics, the returned object identity and the strided path must not change. Rollback: revert to the round-2 solution (sha256 9ca39b9a86a7932e24c872f0b4f9217836fcfa6a4740502c8b70690100f4beff, geo_mean 0.602) if the probe shows the residual cost sits in pybind/CANN and cannot be removed, or if geo_mean does not improve.
success_criteria: Full evaluation PASSED with every correctness workload matched (all 24 correctness cases, required_matched_ratio 1.0), including the 0-element, 1-element, odd-length (1025) and strided cases. In-place contract preserved: the argument is the returned object, its storage is modified, and the strided path still routes through _log10_strided.

The nine workloads with numel <= 1M each show eval latency below 16us (from 17.8-20.2us), which requires the profiler-confirmed non-kernel share to shrink rather than the kernel time.

If the probe finds the residual cost is inside pybind/CANN rather than the Python path, record that as a negative result and stop trimming the host path instead of re-evaluating further micro-optimisations.

data.performance_interpretation: No profiler counter, pipeline, or instruction evidence exists for this round: all six msprof collections (four workloads, then a single retry of the two key workloads) returned status=failed with an empty artifacts list and the identical error 'msprof base collection exited successfully without profile completion marker'. The service still declares profiler=msprof with levels metrics/instruction and capabilities performance_counters, pipeline_utilization, kernel_profile, instruction_listing, so this is a collection failure on the target, not a declaration that profiling is unsupported. Interpretation below therefore rests only on the authoritative get_profile_context eval numbers and is explicitly not profiler-verified. The round-2 eval splits the twelve timing workloads into two distinct regimes. (a) NINE LAUNCH-FLOOR WORKLOADS, 1024 to 1048576 elements across fp16/bf16/fp32 (timing-0,1,2,4,5,6,8,9,10): candidate latency is 11.5-13.1 us and reference 8.9-11.0 us, i.e. a candidate floor near 11.5-13.1 us that is essentially flat over a 1024x input-size range while the reference still moves with size. A candidate latency that does not track input size over three orders of magnitude is consistent with host-side cost dominating, which is directionally the frozen hypothesis (nine of twelve host-launch bound), but no device-task timing was obtained this round to confirm how much of that floor is the compiled launch versus the wrapper prelude. The round-2 prelude rewrite did move seven of these nine down by 0.65-2.32 us (timing-4 -2.32 us, timing-5 -1.91 us, timing-6 -1.80 us, timing-10 -1.20 us, timing-8 -1.08 us, timing-0 -1.08 us, timing-2 -1.00 us), which is consistent with removing Python work from the call path. (b) THREE LARGE WORKLOADS AT numel=16777216 (4096x4096), all 512 programs under BLOCK_MAX=32768: fp16 36.01 us (0.4403), bf16 38.09 us (0.6654), fp32 53.08 us (0.4908) against references 15.85, 25.34 and 26.05 us. Their latency is 2.3-3.0x the launch floor and scales with bytes per element (fp16 36.0 < bf16 38.1 < fp32 53.1 at identical element count), so a host-side prelude cannot explain a 20-27 us gap; the limiting work is on the device path. These three cases carry the worst speedups and are the only place where a large geo_mean gain is available: closing fp16 and fp32 to reference parity alone would be worth roughly +7% and +6% on geo_mean respectively. One anomaly is unexplained by the round-2 diff: timing-11 (fp32 4096x4096) moved from 38.92 us to 53.08 us (+14.16 us, +36.4%) although the change touched only the host prelude and left kernel, tile and grid identical, while timing-3 and timing-7 stayed flat to within 0.05%. Either run-to-run variance at that size or an unobserved specialization effect; it must not be attributed to the prelude rewrite without measurement. VERDICT ON THE FROZEN HYPOTHESIS: neither supported nor contradicted. The eval deltas on the nine small workloads are consistent with it and the change produced geo_mean 0.6958 -> 0.7233 (+3.94%), but the compiled-launch share of the ~12 us floor was not measured this round, and the hypothesis says nothing about the three 4096x4096 cases that now dominate the loss.

next_experiment.action_description: Leave the host fast path, the masked path and the strided path exactly as they are, and change only the aligned large-input geometry: for contiguous inputs with numel >= 16777216 (the three 4096x4096 cases), have each program consume K=2 consecutive BLOCK_MAX tiles through a compile-time unrolled loop, halving grid from n//BLOCK to n//(2*BLOCK)=256 while every inner tile keeps its current 32768-element shape, so no single live buffer grows. Use n % (K*BLOCK) == 0 as the guard and fall back to the existing single-tile launch otherwise.
next_experiment.expected_impact: If the 20-27 us gap on the 4096x4096 cases is per-program setup plus fine-grained DMA rather than saturated HBM bandwidth, halving the program count should shorten those three cases measurably (fp16 36.0 us and fp32 53.1 us are the targets) and lift geo_mean above the current 0.7232637007603351. If the large cases are bandwidth-saturated, latency and geo_mean will be flat, which refutes the granularity mechanism and redirects the next trial to the log/convert instruction expansion instead.

Both the correctness contract and the nine small launch-floor workloads are untouched by construction, but any accidental change to _pick_block or the fast-path key would hit them. Keep a copy of the current main.py before editing; rollback is restoring grid = n//block with a single tile per program and re-running the full eval.

data.performance_interpretation: No profiler counters were obtained, so the following is derived from the authoritative round-1 eval (all 36 cases PASS, geo_mean 0.7301) plus grid arithmetic over the frozen source; treat it as inference, not measurement. Two regimes are visible. (1) Nine workloads, numel 1024..1048576 across fp16/bf16/fp32, sit on a flat plateau of 15.97-17.51 us; for fp32 it is 16.110 us at numel=1024 versus 16.112 us at numel=1048576, so 1000x more elements adds 0.002 us and a fixed per-call cost near 16 us (against an 11.83-14.23 us reference) sets these cases, with the device kernel off the critical path. Headroom is at most ~4 us per call and the seed has already replaced the JIT wrapper with a cached raw launcher, so further host shaving has limited ceiling. (2) The three 4096x4096 workloads cost 81.9 (fp16), 83.2 (bf16) and 82.7 (fp32) us. Doubling moved bytes from 67 MB to 134 MB changes wall time by +0.75 percent, so these cases are NOT bandwidth-bound; subtracting the ~16 us fixed term implies about 66 us of device work and logical rates of 1.02 TB/s (fp16) and 2.03 TB/s (fp32), the latter high enough that the working set is plausibly L2-resident (L2 = 176 MB). Time therefore tracks element count and program count, not bytes: the frozen source launches exactly n/8192 single-tile programs, which is 2048 programs, i.e. ~102 waves on the 20-core device, each a strictly serialized load->compute->store with no loop to overlap MTE2 with VEC. The reference shows the inverted ordering, fp32 fastest at 49.4 us, so it is not byte-bound either. Estimated geo_mean ceilings: 0.903 if only the nine flat workloads reached parity, 0.808 if only the three large ones did, about 0.98 if the large shapes fell to ~30 us. The single highest-value experiment is therefore the persistent multi-tile loop, because the large-shape gap (up to 1.67x) exceeds the per-call host gap (~1.3x), it attacks the largest absolute latencies, and it is falsifiable with one closed-form geometry change. The alternative axis, kept as a fallback only if this experiment falsifies, is reducing per-element vector work for fp16/bf16 by avoiding the blanket fp32 upcast and the unfolded exp form.

next_experiment.action_description: In the aligned contiguous fast path only, replace one-monolithic-tile-per-program with a small fixed number of programs whose body loops over consecutive 8192-element tiles: add @triton.jit _selu_persistent(X, NTILES: tl.constexpr, BLOCK: tl.constexpr) with 'for i in tl.range(0, NTILES)' and offs = (pid*NTILES + i)*BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK), keeping the identical body 1.0507009873554805*tl.where(x>0, x, 1.6732632423543772*(tl.exp(x)-1.0)) and the identical in-place store. data.performance_interpretation: TERMINAL OUTCOME IS A COLLECTION FAILURE, NOT A MEASURED BOTTLENECK. Five msprof attempts (two metrics rounds covering four workloads, plus one instruction round and one isolated metrics retry on selu_-timing-11) all returned status=failed with error 'msprof base collection exited successfully without profile completion marker', per-profile capabilities empty, zero artifacts, and only the six manifest.json files on disk. Nothing was ever executed and parsed from the device counters, so this analysis contains NO profiler facts and NO artifact-backed findings; every statement below is derived only from the authoritative eval comparison in get_profile_context. PROCEDURAL CAVEAT worth checking first on the next attempt: round 2's candidate deliberately routes the hot path through a raw pybind launcher (compiled.run.launch) rather than Triton's NPULauncher dispatch, and _make_contig_launch() aborts to the ordinary launch only when enable_msprof_register_tensor is set. If the harness enables that flag the fallback should trigger, but if msprof instead instruments at a layer this raw call bypasses, msprof would complete with no operator records, which is exactly the symptom observed. This is a hypothesis about the failure, not a measurement, and it is untested. FROZEN-HYPOTHESIS VERDICT: the profiler evidence neither supports nor contradicts the round-2 hypothesis (host-dispatch removal helps only the nine launch-bound workloads); the profiler evidence is simply absent. The EVAL evidence supports it decisively. Before/after per workload: the nine small/medium cases fell from 15.97-17.51 us to 8.96-10.38 us (-37% to -49%, speedups 0.73-0.84 -> 1.03-1.23), while the three 4096x4096 cases moved by at most 0.39% (timing-3 -0.39%, timing-7 -0.02%, timing-11 -0.03%). That is the predicted signature: a pure host-side win capped by the residual call path, leaving device-bound work untouched. geo_mean 0.73012 -> 1.00156 (+37.18%). REGIME SPLIT FROM EVAL TIMING ALONE. (a) Launch-bound regime, nine workloads: latency is flat in numel, e.g. fp16 1024 elements 8.963 us versus fp16 1048576 elements 9.081 us - 1024x more data for +1.3% time - so the ~9-10 us floor is still call overhead, not device work; the remaining headroom here is host-side only and small in geo_mean terms. (b) Device-bound regime, three workloads: 81.61 us (fp16), 83.23 us (bf16), 82.66 us (fp32) at identical element count of 16777216. Converting to element rate gives 205.6, 201.6 and 203.0 Gelem/s - constant within 2.4% while the bytes moved differ by exactly 2x (67.1 MB vs 134.2 MB round trip). A memory-bandwidth-limited kernel cannot hold element rate constant while doubling bytes, and the declared target L2 is 176160768 bytes (168 MB), which exceeds the 134.2 MB fp32 working set, so HBM saturation is not the explanation either. The element rate is constant, therefore the limit scales with ELEMENTS, not bytes. The strongest candidate mechanism is per-element Vector-pipeline work: _selu_nomask() upcasts to fp32 three times in one expression (x.to(tl.float32) in the predicate, then twice inside tl.where, at lines 56/66/122) and evaluates tl.exp unconditionally on the whole 8192-lane fp32 tile, so fp16/bf16 inputs still pay full-width fp32 vector ops. CONSISTENCY WITH THE REFERENCE. The reference achieves 295.5 (fp16), 283.8 (bf16) and 339.9 (fp32) Gelem/s, i.e. 1.44x, 1.41x and 1.67x our element rate, and - informatively - the reference's fp32 case (49.36 us) is FASTER than its fp16 (56.77 us) and bf16 (59.11 us) cases despite moving twice the bytes. A vendor kernel whose cost tracks element count and whose fp32 case is cheapest is consistent with native-dtype vector math, again arguing against a bandwidth limit in either implementation. CAUTION: the same element-count constancy is also predicted by a per-program/per-tile fixed-overhead limit, because all three large cases use the identical grid of 2048 programs (n=16777216, _pick_block returns _BLOCK_MAX=8192). The eval data cannot separate 'per-element fp32 vector work' from 'per-program overhead' - only a device counter capture or a deliberate tile-count change can. That ambiguity is the main open question and the next experiment is built to resolve it.

findings.inference: At identical shape and program count, the vector pipeline is the largest single contributor for float16 (18.03 us of 32.45 us AIV active time) and bfloat16 (22.26 us of 36.87 us), while float32 needs only 12.96 us. Normalized per element, the 2-byte paths cost 1.07 ns and 1.33 ns versus 0.77 ns for float32, i.e. 1.4x-1.7x more vector work although they move half the bytes. The kernel body computes tl.log(x)*C on a value that Triton promotes to fp32 and then casts back with y.to(X.dtype.element_ty) (main.py:60-61), so the most plausible explanation is two extra conversion passes over all 16.7M elements; a dtype-dependent log lowering is an alternative. This is an inference, not a measured fact: the instruction listing that would show the conversions failed (simulator deadline). The practical consequence is that timing-3's own vector activity (18.03 us) already exceeds its entire reference latency (15.86 us from the eval comparison), so load/compute/store overlap alone cannot bring that workload to parity - improving overlap has to be combined with, or bounded by, this per-element vector floor.

findings.label: At identical element count and identical logical bytes, the non-fp16 fp32-math path costs 2.08x the fp16 vector time

findings.inference: timing-3 and timing-7 move the same 67,108,864 logical bytes over the same 16,777,216 elements and launch a pure vector kernel, yet the vector pipe is active 27.21us in the fp16 case and 56.66us in the bf16 case. Per element that is 2.08x. Because bf16 and fp32 run the same fp32 expression while only bf16 pays the bf16->fp32 and fp32->bf16 conversion passes, the fp32 case (2.759 ns/Kelem) is the cleaner estimate of the pure fp32-expression cost and the extra 0.618 ns/Kelem on bf16 (~22% of its vector time) is attributable to the two conversion passes; the remaining ~1.70x over fp16 is the cost of evaluating the curve in fp32 instead of fp16. Decisive scale check: the candidate's vector pipe alone (56.66us) is essentially the entire reference latency for timing-7 (59.03us), and for timing-11 the vector pipe (46.29us) is likewise essentially the reference's 49.30us. So the 1.4-1.7x large-case gap cannot be closed by launch or blocking parameters; it requires reducing per-element vector work. Logical throughput is derived from the frozen spec, not measured physical HBM bytes, and no calibrated bandwidth ceiling was obtained, so no saturation or Roofline claim is made.

findings.label: Scalar prologue cost is purely per-program; the 8192 block cap doubles it on bf16/fp32 without evidence of internal sub-tiling

evidence.metric: derived aiv_scalar_time per program, fp16 / bf16 / fp32

findings.inference: Scalar active time scales with program count, not with element count: 5.8355us at 1024 programs versus 12.4634/12.8398us at 2048 programs, i.e. 5.7-6.3ns per program regardless of dtype or per-program tile size. The block cap of 8192 for the non-fp16 dtypes therefore costs roughly 6.6us of extra scalar work on the 4096x4096 cases. The per-program scalar cost being constant across two different tile sizes (16384 fp16 elements vs 8192 bf16 elements) is evidence against significant multi-buffer-induced internal sub-tiling in the 8192-element programs; small within-program loop overhead would show up as a higher per-program cost at the larger tile. This is medium confidence because internal sub-tiling can only be settled with IR/instruction mapping, which was not collected. Note also that this scalar saving is bounded: halving programs would not touch the vector floor above.

findings.label: fp32 keeps the same per-program tile as fp16 in bytes but spends 3.9x the MTE2 active time of bf16

findings.inference: timing-11 and timing-3 both move 32 KiB per program, and timing-7 moves 16 KiB per program, so fp32's per-transfer size is not smaller than fp16's. Nevertheless fp32's MTE2 pipe is active 27.36us versus 9.45us for bf16 at the same 2048 program count, and versus 7.02us for fp16 at 1024 programs. fp32's logical effective throughput (1.383 TB/s) is close to fp16's (1.464 TB/s) while bf16 sits at 0.805 TB/s, so the fp32 case moves its 2x bytes at nearly the fp16 rate while bf16 is well below both: this is consistent with bf16 being held back by per-element vector conversion cost rather than by transfer, and with fp32 approaching a transfer-related limit. This cannot be promoted to a bandwidth-saturation or bytes-per-MTE2 claim because GM_to_UB/UB_to_GM byte counters, aiv_mte2/aiv_mte3 instruction counts, bank-conflict ratio and any calibrated hardware bandwidth ceiling were not collected in this round.

findings.inference: bf16 (83.544 us device) and fp16 (45.860 us device) move the same interface byte volume, so the 1.82x device-time gap cannot be transfer; it is the vector pipe, whose time is 2.08x (56.66 vs 27.21 us) and whose share rises to 66-68% of aiv_time. findings.label: Eval latency is flat across 1024 to 1M elements while the device kernel spans 2.8-26.5 us, so per-call host work dominates every workload

findings.inference: Authoritative eval latencies from get_profile_context are 0.0979-0.1039 ms for all nine timing workloads, i.e. the 1M cases (98.3-102.8 us) are no slower than the 1024 cases (97.9-99.0 us) even though their device kernel is 9.5x larger (26.4 us vs 2.8 us). Because the same source issues exactly one `_uniform_kernel` device task per call and no auxiliary copies, the invariant ~98 us per call must be host-side: `torch.empty_like`, the `torch_device_fn.current_device()` query, the fresh `_rng_state` read, the three dict lookups and the Triton `_uniform_kernel[grid](*args)` dispatch. Fitting device time inside 98-104 us requires host >=~72-96 us on every workload, so the eval latency floor is set by submission, not by the kernel. Calibrated at high confidence because the flat-latency and single-task facts are direct measurements; the exact host split is not measurable with the capabilities advertised here.

findings.label: Device queue is starved between calls: ~98-135 us of task wait versus 2.8-26.5 us of kernel busy time

evidence.metric: Task Wait Time(us) of steady-state call (1024 float16)
inter-launch interval from Task Start Time(us) row3->row4 (1024 float16)
Task Wait Time(us) of steady-state call (65536 float16)
Task Wait Time(us) of steady-state call (1048576 bfloat16)

findings.inference: In the profiled run the device sits idle 98-135 us before each launch and launches arrive every ~106-148 us, so the AIV cores are busy only ~2% (1024) to ~20% (1M) of the submission cycle. This is queue starvation caused by the host producing work more slowly than the device consumes it, not a barrier or dependency inside the kernel. The profiled interval (~130-140 us) is larger than the eval latency (~98 us) because instrumentation adds overhead, so the two must not be subtracted; the qualitative ordering (device idle >> device busy) is what the artifact supports. Indirectly this also bounds any possible device-side gain: even an instantly-finished kernel could not move eval latency much while submission costs ~98 us.

findings.label: For 1M elements the kernel is vector-compute bound in the mixer, not memory bound: vec ratio ~0.83 versus MTE3 ~0.03 and MTE2 ~0
findings.inference: The 1M kernel spends 22.2-22.7 us in the vector pipe and only 0.76-1.15 us storing; the store grows with dtype width (2 MiB fp16/bf16 vs 4 MiB fp32) while vec time does not, which is the opposite of a bandwidth-limited kernel. Logical output traffic of 2 MiB in 26.4 us is ~80 GB/s of effective write throughput, far under the device's capability and explicitly not named as HBM utilization here because no matched physical-byte counter was read. So the mixer arithmetic (two 32-bit multiplies, three xor-shifts, the sign map and the clamp, plus conversion) is the device limit for this regime. Because the same kernel is only ~27% of the 98-104 us eval latency, this is a secondary opportunity today.

findings.label: In the generated instruction stream the sign map (main.py:90) and the interval clamp (main.py:93) dominate vector cost, and both expand into compare/select/mask plus BAR and flag traffic

evidence.metric: source hotspot cycles for main.py:93 (tl.minimum/tl.maximum clamp), 166 calls
source hotspot cycles for main.py:90 (tl.where sign map), 77 calls
aiv_vec_time_us for the same profiled kernel

findings.inference: For a single 1024-element program the two source lines that implement the sign map and the interval clamp account for 0.92 us of the 1.194 us vector time under simulator scope, emitted as VCMPV/VSEL/MOVEMASK/VMOVMASK_XN/VNOT sequences bracketed by BAR, SET_FLAG and WAIT_FLAG. The mapping `xi<0 ? -xi-1 : xi` exists only to turn the signed word into a magnitude, and the clamp exists only to force the result back inside [lo,hi]; a bit-slice mapping (e.g. consuming the top bits of the mixed word) would remove the branch-and-select entirely, and the clamp is provably redundant whenever the host interval rounding already guarantees the value lands in range. Confidence is medium and scope is one 1024-element program: 616/641 instructions are source-mapped, simulator time is diagnostic only, and this listing was not collected for a 1M program, so the cycle share is not transferable as a measured speedup.

findings.label: The round-4 int32 counter fold removed the int64 device path: all three 1M dtypes run the kernel in 26.33-26.53 us with 32-bit vector instructions

evidence.metric: vector opcode width present in listing (VMULS/VAND/VSHR/VCONV, no 64-bit integer vector op)

findings.inference: The three 1M dtypes differ in output width by 2x yet agree on kernel duration within 0.2 us, which is what a 32-bit-lane arithmetic kernel with a negligible store would produce and is inconsistent with a promoted 64-bit path. Round 3 measured 0.746 ms on these same 1M cases; round 4 measures 98.3-102.8 us of eval latency and 26.3-26.5 us of device kernel, so the frozen hypothesis (fold the counter epoch into the key to keep seed/off below 2**31) is supported by these measurements. The instruction listing is from the 1024-element program, so the width claim is scoped there and combined with the dtype-invariance measurement rather than asserted on its own.

findings.label: The 0.891 and 0.947 low scores are reference-side measurement variance, not a slow candidate case

evidence.metric: min_duration_us / max_duration_us of _uniform_kernel across 100 invocations (1048576 bfloat16)
min_duration_us / max_duration_us of _uniform_kernel across 100 invocations (1048576 float16)

findings.inference: The two lowest-speedup workloads are the most device-stable ones (3% spread over 100 invocations) and their candidate eval latencies, 0.0983 and 0.1028 ms, sit inside the 0.0979-0.1039 ms band that the other seven workloads occupy. Their speedups are low because the reference side measured fast in those runs (0.0876 and 0.0974 ms) while the highest-speedup float32 1M case measured a slow 0.1089 ms reference with an almost identical candidate latency (0.0999 ms). So the residual spread of the round is reference-side jitter of roughly +-10%, and bfloat16 1M should not be treated as a defective kernel regime.

data.performance_interpretation: Round 4 passes with geo_mean 1.0254 (from 0.5048 at the round-2 baseline) and every timing workload between 0.891x and 1.090x, so the frozen int32 counter-fold hypothesis was correct and the round-3 int64 collapse is gone. The profiler shows why the score stops near 1.0 rather than climbing: the candidate's device work is now tiny (2.79 us at 1024, 7.61 us at 65536, 26.4 us at 1M) but its eval latency is pinned at 97.9-103.9 us for every size and dtype, and the per-call device queue shows 98-135 us of idle wait against 2.8-26.5 us of kernel busy time. The remaining cost is the host submission path of one Triton dispatch per call plus output allocation, device query, bounds/tile lookups and the host RNG counter. Because the reference implementation is also pinned in the same 87.6-108.9 us band with only ~5.5 us of device work in three tasks, the match is a tie between two host-bound implementations; beating it requires going below the ~98 us submission cost, not improving the kernel. Device-side headroom exists only in the 1M regime (26.4 us, vector-bound at ratio 0.83 with the sign map and clamp as the largest vector contributors) and would become relevant only after the host floor is cut.

Latency fell on exactly the three workloads the frozen plan targets: timing-3 (f16 4096x4096) 45.61 -> 41.88us (-8.2%, 1.359x vs reference), timing-7 (bf16 4096x4096) 83.25 -> 75.51us (-9.3%), timing-11 (f32 4096x4096) 82.71 -> 72.87us (-11.9%). The hypothesis that per-program tile cost limits the 16M cases is therefore supported by eval latency for the large regime and unsupported for the 1024/65536 regime, where a launch-side residual remains. It must not be upgraded to a device-level mechanism: no pipeline ratios, MTE/Vector activity or instruction counts were obtained, and the reference for timing-3 is itself slower (56.92us) than for timing-11 (49.32us), so the 1.359x cannot be read as a faster compute body.

findings.inference: Only about 15% of the complete 1024-element call is device execution. Because the 65536-element cases in the same round show the same ~0.070 ms eval latency (get_profile_context) while this 1024 case already costs 10.77 us on device, the residual ~59 us is per-call host work that does not scale with element count: output allocation (main.py:258), generator state read/advance (main.py:275-277) and the launch submission of the direct-entry closure (main.py:239-241). The direct-entry path demonstrably took effect (eval latency fell 0.1113 -> 0.0700 ms versus round 2 on this case), so the Triton metacall is no longer the dominant host term. The split inside the remaining ~59 us cannot be attributed with these artifacts: the timeline carries no host API durations and the msprof log reports no host summary, so naming allocation, generator state or launch submission as the single cause would be unsupported.

findings.label: Three 1M-element cases are device-bound and vector-pipe bound: eval latency equals kernel duration, vector ratio 0.88-0.90 with MTE2 ~0 and MTE3 <=2.5%
findings.backend_detail: Grid = cdiv(n, BLOCK*4) with BLOCK=4096 at 1M elements -> 64 programs; vector ratio is a marginal pipe-activity ratio, not peak utilization and not a time decomposition.

evidence.value: 64 in 110/110 invocations for each of timing-2 and timing-5 and timing-8

findings.inference: For these three cases eval latency and device duration coincide (85.25 vs 84.28; 87.99 vs 86.41; 86.91 vs 86.45 us), so host submission is fully overlapped and only device time matters. The kernel is arithmetic-bound in the vector pipe rather than bandwidth-bound: there are no input reads (MTE2 = 0.012 us) and MTE3 traffic of 1.3-2.1 us covers a 2 MiB output, which is far below this device's achievable bandwidth for an 84 us window. The work is the fully unrolled Philox4x32-10 (main.py:64-89, 10 static rounds with two mul_hi_lo splits each) plus uint_to_uniform_float scaling and a two-sided clamp (main.py:116-119). With vector busy 0.88-0.90 and scalar 7.4%, at most roughly 10% of the kernel window is not attributed to a busy pipe, so any device-side gain on these three cases must come from reducing arithmetic per element, not from more parallel programs or better DMA.

findings.inference: _plan picks BLOCK = clamp(next_pow2(n/160), 64, 4096) = 64 and grid = cdiv(1024, 256) = 4, i.e. 256 elements per program on a 20-core device. Per-program vector plus scalar time is ~7.9 us for only 256 outputs, versus ~1.5 ns per output in the 1M regime, which indicates a large fixed per-program cost (unrolled Philox prologue and index setup) rather than element-proportional work. This makes finer program granularity tempting, but it cannot improve these cases in this round: the complete call is host-bound at 70 us, so reducing 10.77 us of device time changes nothing measurable.

Both readings are consistent with an instruction-footprint effect, but no instruction-level artifact was collected in this round, so I do not treat this as a cause and would not act on it before the host question is resolved.

data.performance_interpretation: Round 3 splits the nine timing workloads into two regimes, so the frozen hypothesis is only half supported. Supported: for the six 1024/65536 cases the device work is small and the call is host-bound. timing-0 confirms it directly (10.77 us device inside a 70.02 us eval call, ~70 us of stream idle per invocation). Contradicted: for the three 1M-element cases the device kernel is 84.3-86.5 us and eval latency is 85.3/88.0/86.9 us, i.e. the call is device-bound; the hypothesis that all nine are launch-bound does not hold there. The eval-side numbers are also flat across dtype and size in the first two size classes (0.0693-0.0705 ms for 1024 and 65536 elements), which is itself evidence that a per-call host floor, not element count, sets those six latencies. Relative positioning versus the reference is therefore inverse to device work: the six host-bound cases are the round's wins (1.59-1.81x) and the three device-bound cases are the drag (1.13-1.28x), and the reference itself shows a flat ~0.096-0.127 ms floor. The largest remaining lever is the ~59 us unattributed host term (worth roughly +20-25% geo_mean if even 20 us of it is removable), because the device-bound cases expose at most ~10% unaccounted vector/scalar slack and reducing Philox arithmetic would require changing generator semantics, which the campaign forbids. All timings above are diagnostic; authoritative latency remains the get_profile_context walltime (geo_mean 1.4926, before 0.8924).

If no ablation exceeds a few microseconds, stop host work and record the launch floor as measured rather than guessed.

findings.label: Per-program fixed cost dominates device scaling: 512-element programs cost 3.23 us/program while 2048-element programs cost only 6.15 us/program
findings.backend_detail: msprof aiv_time/aiv_scalar_time consistently track the fitted fixed share (aiv_scalar_time 17.66 us small, 216.32 us large).
findings.inference: Row geometry from the source: timing-4 uses BR=8, IWP=64 (512 input elements per program, 256 programs) and timing-3 uses BR=16, IWP=128 (2048 input elements per program, 2048 programs); both match the Block Num column exactly. Dividing kernel time by programs/20 cores gives 3.23 us (small) and 6.15 us (large) per program, i.e. a 4x increase in tile elements yields only 1.9x more per-program time. A two-point linear fit is ~2.24 us fixed + ~1.9 ns per input element per program, which attributes roughly 29/41 us of the small kernel and 229/630 us of the large kernel to per-program cost. The dtype differs between the two fixtures (fp32 vs bf16), which weakens the fit, so this is an inference rather than a decomposition.

findings.label: Large fixture is device-bound and vector-pipeline dominated; contiguous stores are cheap and the row-gather loads are secondary
findings.backend_detail: Ratios are marginal pipeline-active statistics and are not added into a time decomposition; vec+scalar happens to be close to the kernel duration (631.7 us vs 629.8 us) in this sample, which is treated only as a lead.
findings.inference: The eval latency for this fixture (0.6316 ms) equals the profiled kernel duration (0.6298 ms), so this regime is device-bound. The contiguous join/store path costs only 8.2 us of MTE3 while the vector stage is 415 us, and the two row-gather loads cost 179 us of MTE2, so the interpolation arithmetic and index handling on fp32 tiles (vertical blend, two tl.gather calls, even/odd blend, join, dtype convert) are the element-proportional cost, not the output write. Logical traffic is about 16.8 MB read + 16.8 MB written in 630 us, so this kernel is far from a bandwidth limit; no Roofline claim is made.

findings.label: Small fixtures still spend more than half of eval latency outside the device kernel, even though the kernel itself is also inefficient
findings.backend_detail: One kernel per call (operation_count=1); no extra cast/TransData stages in the candidate path.
findings.inference: Eval latency for this fixture is 0.1024 ms while the single profiled device kernel is 41.42 us, so roughly 60 us of each call is outside the kernel (allocation plus Python/JIT dispatch in run()); the profiler run itself inflates host gaps, so this is a qualitative split from two independent collections, not a subtraction-validated decomposition. Round 3 already removed 23.9-29.9% of the small-case latency by caching metadata-derived launch parameters, which confirms the host path is a real and still large contributor. Separately, the 41.4 us kernel is about 3.3x the vendor ResizeBilinearV2 stage seen for the same geometry in the round-2 paired reference trace, so host-only work cannot reach the 0.8x target: this kernel's device time alone exceeds the reference total (30.3 us).

data.performance_interpretation: Round 3 raised geo_mean from 0.3033 to 0.3450 (geo_mean_delta_pct 13.73). All of the gain came from the three small fixtures (latency -23.9% to -29.9%), which is consistent with the launch-parameter cache removing host work; the three large fixtures moved by less than 0.2% and remain device-bound (timing-3: 0.6298 ms kernel vs 0.6316 ms eval). The frozen hypothesis (small fixtures dominated by per-call Python parameter derivation) is therefore supported for the host part but incomplete: after the cache, ~60 us of host time per small call remains, and the small kernel itself (41.4 us) is still ~3.3x the vendor resize stage. Both regimes show a large aiv_scalar share (0.43 small, 0.34 large) and a program-count/tile-size relation that implies a per-program fixed cost of roughly 2.2 us, so the next lever is device-side amortization, not further parameter derivation.

data.performance_interpretation: Round 2's frozen hypothesis is supported by the authoritative eval: contiguous multi-KB block loads cut the large geometries from about 0.629 ms to 0.264-0.278 ms (timing-1 0.329x -> 0.783x, timing-5 0.347x -> 0.816x, timing-3 0.435x -> 0.954x) and geo_mean from 0.5756 to 0.9345. The small geometries (0.0308-0.0322 ms, 0.89-1.26x) are host/launch bound and already at or above reference, so the whole remaining deficit sits on timing-1/3/5 and equals about 57, 13 and 50 us respectively. Structural reading of the delivered source: every GM address in _blk2x_kernel is affine (two contiguous multi-KB loads, two 2-D stores with row stride 2*OW), so the only data-dependent, non-affine operations left are the four axis-1 tl.gather calls that produce the +-1 column neighbours, plus the tile-wide mixes and join/reshape interleaves that consume them. That makes the horizontal stage, not data movement, the place to test next. This is a source-level inference, not a measurement: the profiler produced no AIV/MTE counters this round, so it neither confirms nor refutes the split between vector, scalar and MTE time, and it cannot say whether the gathers lower to a per-lane scalar loop or a vector shuffle.

next_experiment.action_description: Keep _blk2x_kernel's block geometry, two contiguous block loads, stores and all fallback paths unchanged, and replace the four (QB,IW) axis-1 gathers per program with two gathers on doubled-width interleaved tiles. Build Qf = tl.reshape(tl.join(vf, vf), (QB, OW)) and Qo = tl.reshape(tl.join(vo, vo), (QB, OW)) once per program, then take both column neighbours from a single gather per source tile with the parity permutation P where P[2k] = max(2k-2, 0) and P[2k+1] = min(2k+2, OW-1). The output tile becomes 0.75*Q + 0.25*tl.gather(Q, P, 1), stored directly with the same (QB,OW) rows and row stride 2*OW, so the two even/odd mix pairs and the two post-mix join/reshape interleaves disappear. This is option (a), tested in its cheapest falsifiable form.
next_experiment.expected_impact: Halves the gather operation count (4 -> 2) at unchanged gathered-element volume and removes the two post-mix joins. If the gather cost is dominated by per-operation setup/control, large-case latency falls by 30-60 us: timing-1 from 0.264 ms toward 0.20-0.23 ms (0.783x -> about 0.90-1.00x), with similar movement on timing-3 and timing-5, moving geo_mean from 0.9345 toward 1.00-1.05. If the cost is per-element, the change is neutral - that is the falsification, and it redirects effort to mix/join vector work or a cube formulation.
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: The gather index must match the source on every non-axis dimension and the axis must stay minor; the parity permutation must clamp both ends so no lane leaves the tile, or boundary values differ from PyTorch's i1p rule. Doubled-width (QB,2IW) tiles raise UB pressure even though they replace the existing post-mix (QB,OW) tiles; if QB=16 with IW=128 overflows the 192 KiB UB, verify the compiled buffer report and drop to QB=8 rather than weakening the math. A 2x wider index tensor may hit a backend restriction and must be recorded as a compile failure, not worked around by changing the computation. Keep the round-2 kernel reachable behind a module flag and revert if geo_mean is not strictly better than 0.9345; do not accept a gain that appears only in per-iteration-synced probes.

data.performance_interpretation: Round 1 evaluates clean (27/27, geo_mean 0.6041) but the device side of the question you asked is unmeasured: 5 msprof collection attempts across 3 workloads and both advertised levels all failed with the same missing-completion-marker error, so no counters, no pipeline utilization and no kernel duration exist. What this round does establish is where the time is NOT. Per-call latency is 0.0557-0.0572 ms on all nine timing workloads while data volume spans 256 KiB fp16 (timing-0) to 8 MiB fp32 (timing-8): a 64x change in data moves per-call time by ~1.23x at most, with no size correlation at all (the 256 KiB case is not faster than the 8 MiB case). The same host path is independently measured inside this round's workspace at ~44 us of fixed cost out of ~56 us - 22.58 us for the raw ctypes NPULauncher.launch call, 15.21 us for the two allocations, 6.19 us for the two tensor views - leaving ~12 us of residual Python. Q1 (device-side kernel time per timing workload): not obtained. Q2 (memory bandwidth vs UB tiling/pipeline vs launch/tail): the limiter is host launch cost, not HBM bandwidth and not the MTE2/Vector pipeline. As arithmetic rather than measurement, the kernel issues 2 reads + 1 write per element, i.e. 0.75 MiB (timing-0/3/6), 12 MiB (timing-1/2/4/5) and 24 MiB (timing-7/8) of logical traffic, which at the 728 GB/s that a same-target kernel of this shape reaches on a 32 MiB buffer is ~1 us, ~17 us and ~35 us - every value below the ~56 us host floor, which is exactly why the flat curve is consistent with a fully hidden device term. Grid tail is mild anyway: 32 programs over 20 cores (1.6 waves) for the small shapes, 64-128 programs (3.2-6.4 waves) for the large ones. Q3 (two-pass -> single-pass): the whole tensor is at most 8 MiB against 168 MiB of L2, so the reduce pass can leave it resident and the apply pass's re-read is expected to be an L2 hit. The saving would therefore be L2 bandwidth and a second address/schedule pass, not a doubling of HBM reads - much smaller than the naive 24 MB -> 16 MB traffic reduction suggests, and unconfirmable without L2 hit/miss counters. Explicit conclusion, as requested: the kernel body is not worth optimizing this round. Any device-side win is currently invisible because a ~56 us host floor hides a <=35 us device term, so effort belongs entirely in host overhead until per-call host drops below ~30 us; at that point timing-7 and timing-8 (fp32, ~23-35 us of estimated device work) become the binding term and the single-pass question becomes worth a controlled test. The single highest-value secondary action is restoring profiling compatibility, without which the device side stays dark.

next_experiment.action_description: Do not touch _gn_kernel's body (tiling, BLOCK, grid shape, two-pass structure) this round; the measured host path is the only term large enough to move geo_mean. In run() of main.py make one focused change to the steady-state fast path. (a) Keep allocating the (2,N,G) scratch exactly as today but stop creating the two tensor views: replace `mean = buf[0]; rstd = buf[1]` with mp = buf.data_ptr() and rp = mp + N*group*itemsize and pass both as integers. buf[0] and buf[1] are already views of the same storage today, so this changes nothing semantically; it removes the measured 6.19 us slice2 cost. (b) Hoist the per-call Python that only depends on the specialization into the cached entry: the six data_ptr() calls, the dtype/stride/shape reads and the 20-element key tuple. The steady path should do one dict lookup, read only the six current pointers plus the current stream, and issue the launch from a pre-built positional argument tuple (that residual Python is ~12 us of the 56 us). (c) As a required part of the same edit, when TRITON_REGISTER_TENSOR_MSPROF is set, fall back to the normal _gn_kernel[(group, N)](x, out, mean, rstd, w, b, ...) tensor launch so NPULauncher.__call__ runs and the msprof registration / completion marker is produced; keep the integer fast path for normal execution only.
next_experiment.expected_impact: Host per-call ~56 us -> ~42-46 us (~6 us of tensor views plus ~4-8 us of residual Python), i.e. geo_mean 0.6041 -> ~0.75-0.82 if the host-bound model is right. It also unblocks device-side measurement in the following profile round, which is currently impossible. The prediction has a falsifiable signature: eval latency and the in-process run_cpu_ms/run_ev_ms probe both drop by the same absolute amount while the device-side estimate (~1 us small shapes / ~17 us mid / ~35 us fp32 large) does not change.
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: Keep `out` freshly allocated per call - do not cache the output or input tensors, and never key the cache on element count alone. mean/rstd must stay views of a freshly allocated scratch and remain valid after return. Read the stream per call. The profiler fallback must produce bit-identical numerics and must not double-execute the kernel (compile/warmup only, then exactly one launch). Non-contiguous inputs still need the existing contiguous fallback, and alignment/dtype/stride/affine fields must stay in the cache key. Likely mechanism for the collection failure, from the captured backend source: run() caches (ck.run.launch, ck.function, ck.packed_metadata) and calls the raw ctypes launch with six integer addresses, so NPULauncher.__call__ - the only place that fills packed_metadata['tensor_params_shape'] when TRITON_REGISTER_TENSOR_MSPROF is set and sets triton.backends.ascend.utils.TRITON_PROFILER_REGISTERED - never executes. The collector therefore never sees the completion marker even though the kernel runs correctly. get_tensor_params_shape also needs objects exposing size(), which plain ints do not, so a tensor-arg fallback (not yet attempted) is the natural fix; this is a hypothesis with source-level support, not a proven sole cause.

data.performance_interpretation: No profiler counter backs the numbers below; only trusted eval data from get_profile_context is used. Round 1 is the frozen baseline and the round-1 candidate is the seed source verbatim (manifest request.implementation.sources[0].content equals the seed text, identity.solution_sha256=d6aff85c...). All 18 correctness workloads PASSED and all 9 timing workloads PASSED, geo_mean=0.5917464299202004, with every timing workload slower than the ATen reference. The decisive measured pattern is latency invariance to work size: input payload spans 0.25 MiB (timing-0/3, fp16/bf16 4x32x32x32 = 131,072 elements), 0.5 MiB (timing-6, fp32 same shape), 4 MiB (timing-1/2/4/5, 2,097,152 fp16/bf16 elements) and 8 MiB (timing-7/8, 2,097,152 fp32 elements) - a 32x spread - while candidate latency moves only between 0.05357 ms (timing-7) and 0.06143 ms (timing-1), a 1.15x spread, and the reference moves 0.03263-0.03676 ms, a 1.13x spread. A bandwidth- or compute-limited kernel cannot be flat over a 32x payload change, so device work is a small part of the ~56 us call and a fixed per-call term dominates. The candidate-minus-reference delta is systematic in every workload: 23.84, 28.04, 20.61, 22.63, 23.35, 25.93, 20.44, 20.94 and 23.23 us for timing-0..8 (mean ~23.2 us, spread ~7.4 us) across that 32x payload range, isolating a roughly constant ~20-28 us of extra per-call cost relative to the reference. In source terms that points at host-side work in run(): two torch.empty allocations (out plus a (2,N,group) buffer followed by two Python-level buf[0]/buf[1] views), six data_ptr() calls, a 20-element tuple key rebuilt every call, a dict lookup, then the compiled-kernel launch entry. The ~6.5 us device duration quoted in the seed docstring and the VECTOR/MTE2/MTE3 active ratios in the supplied starting-point context were not re-measured this round and are not round-1 evidence, though their magnitude is consistent with the flat-latency pattern. Confidence in 'launch' as dominant_bound is medium: it rests on eval-latency size-invariance plus a matching per-workload delta, not on device counters.

findings.inference: For timing-11 the four AIV pipe times sum to 41.23 us against aiv_time 40.909 us, i.e. the pipes occupy disjoint intervals and provide no overlap; the kernel is 'busy' ~98% of its duration yet the critical path is the sum of four serial stages, not the maximum. The same additive pattern holds at fp16 (20.97 us sum vs 20.83 us aiv_time). Each program in _neg_exact handles exactly one tile with no loop (main.py:44-47), so Triton has no opportunity to software-pipeline the next load against the current negate/store. If the pipes overlapped, the bound would fall to max(MTE2, MTE3, VEC) ~12.6 us for fp32 and ~6.4 us for fp16. Eval latency here (41.449 us) matches the device duration, confirming this is the one workload where device time, not dispatch, sets the score.

data.performance_interpretation: Round 3 eval (fingerprint 2a97cc87..., geo_mean 0.41288 vs 0.28315 in round 2, +45.8%) splits the twelve timed workloads into two clearly separated regimes. Regime A, nine workloads (all shapes except 4096x4096): fp16/bf16/fp32 at 1024, 65536 and 1048576 elements. Their device kernels take 1.5-5.2 us, yet eval latency is 30.3-31.5 us, and same-acquisition task-start cadence is 39.7-45.4 us, so the vector core is idle for most of every iteration; latency is set by the per-call launch path, which costs ~18-19 us more than the aten reference's 11.1-12.9 us. These nine workloads contribute the bulk of geo_mean and are where the remaining headroom is (each could approach speedup 1.0). Regime B, three workloads (4096x4096 fp32/fp16/bf16): device time 41.8/22.0/34.2 us matches or nearly matches eval latency 41.4/30.4/34.0 us, so here device work sets the score. In this regime the four AIV pipes are serialized (their times sum to aiv_time), the 64 KiB tile already achieves ~5.9-6.0 TB/s L2-resident reads, and bf16 pays a further 3.9x vector-time penalty versus fp16. Verdict on the frozen hypothesis: the retile prediction is supported. It forecast 152 us -> 34-42 us for the large workloads with the nine host-bound ones staying at 31-36 us and geo_mean ~0.42; measured results are 30.4/34.0/41.4 us for the large ones and 30.3-31.5 us for the nine, with geo_mean 0.4129. Its stated mechanism, however, is only partially right: the gain came from fewer programs at an already near-ceiling per-program DMA rate, and the residual device time is a pipe-serialization problem rather than a bandwidth shortfall.

Hoist the device index and current-stream lookups out of the per-call path, and avoid rebuilding the tuple key and re-calling A.is_contiguous()/_device_index() where the value is already known for that specialization. Keep the 64 KiB tiling, the exact/tail/strided kernel split, in-place storage semantics, stride handling, and the existing run() body intact and reachable as a fallback. Do not change the device kernels in this experiment, so the measurement stays attributable to the host path.

data.performance_interpretation: NO PROFILER COUNTERS WERE OBTAINED THIS ROUND, so questions 1-3 (device vs full-call split, MTE2/MTE3/Vector active ratios, bank-conflict or spill evidence) CANNOT be answered from measurement; any figure for them would be invented. What CAN be established uses only authoritative eval latencies from get_profile_context plus workload specs from hgkda_workloads, with the arithmetic below labeled as inference. (i) Small cases carry almost no device cost: timing-0 is float16 [1024] = 4 KiB read + 4 KiB written = 8 KiB total traffic; at the measured 12.3927 us that is 0.33 GB/s effective, and the 10.2833 us reference on the same 8 KiB shows the harness floor is ~10 us. So essentially all of the 12.4 us and the whole 0.83 speedup is host launch/dispatch cost, and roughly 2.1 us of extra host work versus the reference is the entire small-case deficit. (ii) Large-case cost is byte-driven, not log-instruction-driven: all three large cases execute exactly 16,777,216 tl.log evaluations with an identical op mix modulo dtype conversion, yet candidate per-element time is 2.5519 ns (fp16), 2.6482 ns (bf16, +3.8% at identical bytes) and 4.6094 ns (fp32), i.e. the fp32/fp16 time ratio is 1.806 for a 2.0x per-element byte ratio. Time tracks bytes while the log count is constant, which contradicts competing hypothesis (b) that the tl.log lowering is the dominant limiter. (iii) Logical effective throughput computed as 2 x bytes-per-element x elements / latency: candidate 1.57 TB/s (fp16), 1.51 TB/s (bf16), 1.74 TB/s (fp32); reference 4.24 TB/s, 2.65 TB/s, 5.20 TB/s on the identical shapes, dtypes, in-place storage and measurement harness. Because the reference reaches 2.7-3.0x the candidate's logical rate on the same data, competing hypothesis (d) 'simple GM bandwidth saturation' is contradicted as an explanation of the gap: the memory system demonstrably sustains at least the reference's rate, and the candidate sits near one third of it. (iv) UB pressure, hypothesis (c), has no positive evidence: the fp32 tile is 8192 elements = 32 KiB source and the 2-byte tile 16384 elements = 32 KiB source (64 KiB once staged to fp32), both far below the 192 KiB UB, the kernel compiles and passes all 36 workloads, and fp32 - which uses the SMALLER tile - shows the HIGHEST effective throughput, the opposite of what a large-tile UB-pressure story predicts. (v) That leaves hypothesis (a) as the leading candidate at medium confidence, without counters: with 2048 programs (fp32) and 1024 programs (2-byte) on 20 AI cores the grid is ~51-102 waves, so parallelism is not scarce, but each program performs exactly one monolithic tl.load of the whole tile, one vector chain and one monolithic tl.store, leaving no loop body for Triton's software pipeliner to multi-buffer, so per core the sequence is MTE2-wait -> V -> MTE3-drain with no cross-iteration overlap; the measured 1.5-1.7 TB/s is consistent with approximately serialized transfer phases, whereas full overlap would approach the 2.6-5.2 TB/s the reference demonstrates. The round's frozen hypothesis (strided-path correctness plus a reusable compiled launcher for small shapes) is already settled by the eval rather than by profiling: 36/36 PASSED including correctness-7/15/23, with small-case latency down to the ~12.4 us floor. Profiler evidence therefore neither supports nor contradicts the frozen hypothesis; it is simply unavailable.

next_experiment.action_description: In _log10_flat and _log10_flat_masked, replace the single monolithic tl.load(x_ptr + offs) / tl.store(x_ptr + offs, ...) over the whole BLOCK with an inner loop over sub-tiles inside the same program: keep the outer tile and grid (block = 8192 elements for 4-byte dtypes, 16384 for 2-byte dtypes, grid = cdiv(n, block) as today), and iterate CHUNK = 2048 elements (4-byte) / 4096 elements (2-byte) via 'for k in tl.range(0, BLOCK, CHUNK, num_stages=2)', loading, staging to fp32, computing tl.log(x) * 0.4342944819032518 and storing each CHUNK inside the loop body. Keep the in-place pointer (same address for load and store; each chunk reads and writes only its own disjoint addresses, so there is no loop-carried dependency), keep the fp32 staging that the correctness contract depends on, and keep the mask only on the final partial program (or reuse _log10_flat_masked for that tail) so the fast path stays unmasked. Leave _log10_scaled and _log10_nd untouched. Do not change _pick_block, the entry cache, the stream resolution or the direct-launcher call signature.
next_experiment.expected_impact: Expected effect is derived from eval-latency arithmetic in performance_interpretation, NOT from profiler counters (none were collected this round). If each program's load, compute and store phases begin to overlap across loop iterations, effective logical throughput should move from the measured 1.51-1.74 TB/s toward the 2.65-5.20 TB/s the reference achieves on the identical workloads: timing-11 from 77.3 us toward 45-55 us, timing-3 from 42.8 us toward 28-34 us, timing-7 from 44.4 us toward 30-36 us, for a projected geo_mean of roughly 0.78-0.85 versus the current 0.6799, with timing-0 unchanged because it is entirely host-bound.
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: Risks: (1) the Ascend backend may ignore num_stages or fail to multi-buffer this loop body, in which case the change is performance-neutral and the chunk loop only adds scalar index arithmetic; (2) multi-buffering multiplies UB demand by the stage count - 2 stages x 2048 fp32 would be 16 KiB in plus 8-16 KiB out per buffer, still far below 192 KiB, but confirm no UB overflow before trusting the result; (3) a smaller CHUNK reduces the vector-op width per iteration, which could cost throughput if the vector unit is better fed by one wide op - mitigate by starting at CHUNK=2048/4096 and only then trying 1024 if UB or code size complains. Rollback: this change is confined to the two contiguous-path @triton.jit bodies; keep the current tmp/main.py as the revert point and restore the monolithic single-load body if any large case regresses.

The three 4096x4096 workloads were deliberately held byte-identical, moved by <=0.03%, and now hold the entire remaining gap: fp16 0.610, bf16 0.637, fp32 0.930. The service profiler failed on both attempts with zero artifacts, so the mechanism had to be located from eval arithmetic and in-workspace device probes rather than counters. Two observations reframe the problem. FIRST, tiling and program decomposition are already explored and flat: in probe3.json on the 4096-square fp16 case, masked_32768 baseline 64.92 us, nomask_16384 59.64, stream8k_s1 61.76, stream16k_s2 61.77 at grid 40, multi_32768x4 66.43, nomask_8192 80.11, and stream32k_s2 fails to compile; in probe5.json cur_16384 65.93 vs cur_32768 66.30 for fp16 and 68.22 for bf16, with 65536 tiles failing to compile (ConvertLinalgIRToBinary) for 16-bit inputs, consistent with the 192 KB UB ceiling. A 512-to-1024 program change costs nothing and grid=40 streaming with two stages gains only about 5%, so neither per-program dispatch nor DMA burst granularity is the dominant term, and 65536-element tiles are not even compilable. SECOND, the large-input cost tracks elements rather than bytes: with 16777216 elements in every case, fp16 (0.027846 ms) moves half the bytes of fp32 (0.030973 ms) yet takes 90% of its time, i.e. 1.660 vs 1.846 ps per element, whereas the oracle improves from 1.718 to 1.013 ps per element across the same pair (effective read+write bandwidth: fp16 2.41 vs 3.95 TB/s, fp32 4.33 vs 4.66 TB/s - so fp32 already reaches 93% of the oracle while the 16-bit cases reach 61%). The only dtype-dependent work in the body is the fp32 widen and narrow around the multiply, which is free for fp32 and doubles lane width while adding two conversion passes over a 2x-wide buffer for fp16/bf16; that predicts precisely this pattern, and it also predicts why shrinking transfers did not help. dominant_bound is therefore mixed: host-issue bound and saturated for nine workloads, and per-element vector work rather than bandwidth or dispatch for the three large ones. The next change is arithmetic-only for 16-bit inputs, leaving the host path and the launch structure untouched.

(b) the data falsify the per-call device-synchronization part of (b) - a per-call sync would have added the full 26 us to the 1M call - but the Triton/CANN submission share of the host floor is not separable with the available msprof capabilities, since no host-side summary was exported. data.performance_interpretation: Round 3 is still host-issue bound, and the host path really did shrink. The device kernel is byte-identical in cost: 2.473 / 11.428 / 28.508 us at 1024 / 65536 / 1048576 fp16, 28.699 us at 1M bf16 and 28.454 us at 1M fp32, all within 0.33% of round 2, with the 1M pipeline mix unchanged at 80.4% AIV vector / 17.1% scalar / 3.9% store. All of the 1.4473 -> 1.6405 geo_mean gain is therefore host-side, and the authoritative eval numbers put non-device per-call cost at 61.31 / 52.89 / 37.47 us (1024 / 65536 / 1M fp16), down 6.0-7.8 us in every regime, satisfying round 2's >=5 us criterion. The profiled kernel-start cadence confirms it independently: 78.76 -> 62.93 us at 1024 and 77.27 -> 70.96 at 65536, flat at 1M (~71-73 us in both rounds). Answering the parent's three questions: (1) yes, device duration is unchanged at 2.473 / 11.428 / 28.508 us; (2) yes, non-device time fell absolutely by 6.0-7.8 us everywhere, but the non-device share fell only 3.6-4.9 points at 1M and 0.4 points at 1024, so the share is the wrong statistic at small sizes; (3) the conclusion is supported - fixed submission (22.3 us, flat in argument count) plus mandatory fresh allocation (39.2 us combined) plus the generator accessors (5.21 us) already account for ~44.4 us, 79% of the 56.3 us free-running call, and every remaining hot-path operation is individually sub-microsecond (three tensor property reads with torch.Size/torch.device construction, five memo comparisons, an eight-element list unpack, one _GENS.get, offset integer math, a key-memo comparison, three identity checks, a closure call and a stream getter). No further in-candidate host reduction of practical size can be named from this evidence, so the candidate is at its floor as far as the profile shows. Two qualifications are recorded rather than glossed over: the subtraction-based split is not profiler-proven because msprof exports no host summary, and ~10.7 us of the alloc+launch gap is unattributed and not removable anyway since a fresh contiguous output is mandatory. The recorded next experiment is accordingly the single bounded falsification of that one bucket with an explicit stop rule, not a new optimisation direction.

next_experiment.action_description: Keep uniform_kernel, BLOCK, grid, dtypes and every device instruction byte-identical and touch only the allocation spelling in the hot path. The single unattributed bucket is the 16.3 us gap between launching into a fresh output (39.2 us) and launching into a fixed buffer (22.9 us), of which new_empty measured alone accounts for only 5.6 us - i.e. ~10.7 us appears only when allocation and launch are combined, and the profiled cadence is size-dependent in exactly that pattern (62.93 / 70.96 / 73.21 us for 2 KB / 128 KB / 2 MB outputs). Run one in-situ A/B in the alloc+launch context (not allocation alone, which is how new_empty was measured) over three spellings that each return a fresh contiguous tensor: self.new_empty(shape), torch.empty(shape, dtype=dtype, device=dev), and torch.empty_like(self, memory_format=torch.contiguous_format). Select whichever wins by at least 1 us in that combined context during warm-up, else keep self.new_empty. Do not cache the output tensor, do not cache the stream, and keep the non-contiguous branch that copies through Triton. This is a stop-rule-bounded falsification of the only remaining >=1 us candidate-side hypothesis, not a parameter sweep.
next_experiment.expected_impact: Upper bound is the 10.7 us of alloc+launch interference; realistic expectation is 0-3 us, because the fresh allocation is mandatory and the interference is plausibly driver/allocator bookkeeping rather than candidate Python. If 3 us were recovered, wall would go 63.4-66.0 -> 60.4-63.0 us and geo_mean ~1.6405 -> ~1.70; if 0, the candidate is proven to sit at its floor and host work stops.
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: torch.empty_like(self) copies self's strides, so a strided self would yield a non-contiguous output and re-open the uninitialised-gap bug the current code avoids; it is admissible only with memory_format=torch.contiguous_format and must be re-validated on the layout cases. Any variant must still allocate a fresh tensor per call and read the stream per call. Roll back to the round-3 host path if any eval or supplementary case regresses; the kernel is byte-identical so no numerical risk exists.
success_criteria: All 18 evaluation workloads still PASSED and the supplementary validator still passes 31/31 cases, including the layout, stream and RNG-replay cases.
geo_mean improves from 1.6405 to >1.65 and uniform-timing-0/1 wall time stays at or below 63.78 / 64.31 us; otherwise revert.
A follow-up msprof profile of uniform-timing-2 shows uniform_kernel avg_duration_us still 28.5 +/- 1.0 us, proving the device path was not touched.

Stop rule: if no spelling beats self.new_empty by >=1 us in the alloc+launch context, declare the candidate at its floor, make no further host change, and record the ~10.7 us residual as allocation/interference cost rather than candidate Python.
